provider_query: Jargon File entry that defines yak shaving
answer:
**Jargon File entry (canonical)**

**yak shaving** — [MIT AI Lab, after 2000: orig. probably from a Ren & Stimpy episode.] Any seemingly pointless activity which is actually necessary to solve a problem which solves a problem which, several levels of recursion later, solves the real problem you're working on.

Source: The Jargon File, online edition at catb.org (entry page dated in the file history around the early 2000s). https://www.catb.org/jargon/html/Y/yak-shaving.html

**Other relevant sources (concise)**

1. **Mirror of the same entry** — Same wording: MIT AI Lab after 2000; probably Ren & Stimpy; recursive chain of seemingly pointless but necessary tasks. http://underpop.free.fr/j/jargon/y/yak-shaving.html

2. **ZVON index** — Points to the Jargon File glossary entry for “yak shaving” and the catb.org online file (version noted as 4.4.7 in that index). https://zvon.org/comp/m/yak_shaving.html

3. **TechTarget** — Programming slang for an endless series of small tasks before the next project step; coined by Carlin J. Vieri (MIT, 1990s) from a *Ren & Stimpy* “Yak Shaving Day” bit. https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/yak-shaving

4. **Stack Exchange (Software Engineering)** — Community gloss matching the recursive-prerequisite sense: a seemingly useless task needed for another task that eventually reaches the real goal; can be neutral or a dig at distraction. https://softwareengineering.stackexchange.com/questions/388092/what-exactly-is-yak-shaving

5. **Visual Thesaurus** — Annoying succession of tasks before the real goal; cites MIT / Carlin Vieri and the Jargon File’s Ren & Stimpy link. https://www.visualthesaurus.com/cm/wc/heavy-lifting-and-shaving-yaks-corporate-lingo/

6. **DEV Community** — Sub-tasks that look unrelated but are needed to finish the real work; origin given as an MIT lab. https://dev.to/cerchie/tech-jargon-defined-what-is-yak-shaving-3hj8

7. **Levellers.ai (origin notes)** — Attributes coining to Carlin J. Vieri (MIT AI Lab, 1990s) after *Ren & Stimpy*; cites a 2000 MIT list post by Jeremy H. Brown and notes the Jargon File’s later, cautious wording. https://www.levellers.ai/what-is/yak-shaving

**Note:** Some secondary definitions diverge (for example PCMag ties the phrase to a Sega game and stresses trivial or sidetracking work). The Jargon File definition above is the standard hacker-glossary entry.

results.content:
![Andy Patrizio](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/patrizio_andy.jpg)

By

- [Andy Patrizio](https://www.techtarget.com/contributor/Andy-Patrizio)

Published: Jan 27, 2023

## What is yak shaving?

Yak shaving is programming lingo for the seemingly endless series of small tasks that have to be completed before the next step in a project can move forward. The term is a great example of internet slang making its way into the collective consciousness and being used to describe impediments to coding.

The term was coined by Carlin J. Vieri, a Ph.D. student at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the 1990s, and was inspired by an episode of the Nickelodeon channel's cartoon _The Ren & Stimpy Show_. In the episode, Ren informs the viewers of an upcoming holiday called Yak Shaving Day, where one must leave shaving cream and a razor on the bathroom sink so that, at night, the Shaven Yak can come and leave presents.

Of course, Vieri was being sarcastic, but the term _yak shaving_ caught on. It refers to engaging in a meaningless task that has no obvious relationship to what's supposed to be worked on but may be necessary to troubleshoot a larger problem. The process of making a simple task unnecessarily complicated may also qualify as yak shaving.

A yak is a domesticated, horned, cowlike mammal native to Tibet that looks similar to a Texas longhorn cow -- albeit with shorter horns -- but with a thick, shaggy coat to help cope with the cold climate of Tibet.

## Examples of yak shaving

Examples of yak shaving fall into two categories: procrastination and necessary annoyance. In the case of the former, it's easy to slip into while [working from home](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/feature/15-advantages-and-disadvantages-of-remote-work), where temptations and distractions abound.

For example, procrastination is when there's a report due today, but it seems dull and a waste of time because no one will ever read it. So, it falls to the end of the priority list behind other household chores -- anything to avoid writing the report.

Necessary annoyance occurs when the original goal is to complete task A, but an unforeseen cascade of circumstances intervenes to distract from completing it. Those involved with software development may be especially sensitive to necessary annoyances. For example, a field entry name must be changed in [source code](https://www.techtarget.com/searchapparchitecture/definition/source-code) because it was changed in the database. But, as the software engineer looks into the code, other errors become apparent and need to be corrected. The required changes affect other apps, and then those, in turn, affect yet more applications. That can lead a developer down a rabbit hole of [dependency hell](https://www.techtarget.com/searchitoperations/definition/dependency-hell) that needs to be fixed before making the initial modifications.

## How to avoid yak shaving

Avoiding both types of yak shaving requires self-discipline and self-awareness. In the case of procrastination, it comes down to recognizing it, stopping the time-wasting exercises and getting on with the unpalatable task at hand.

![Steps to avoid yak shaving](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/yak_shaving-f.png)Follow these steps to avoid falling down a rabbit hole.


In the case of distraction, stopping isn't an option because these are necessary steps. Even if a half-dozen other updates occur before making a planned change, they must be done.

It is possible to reduce the distracting effects of yak shaving by reframing the situation. Here are some steps to consider:

1. **Realize you have been sidetracked.** The moment you realize you are moving toward yak shaving, stop.
2. **Understand the task at hand.** You can't get back on track until you realize what the track is. Refocus to become aware of possible distractions.
3. **Have a plan of action.** Once you've recognized you are off course, formulate a [project plan](https://www.techtarget.com/searchcio/definition/project-planning) to get back on course.
4. **Set modest goals.** A series of small tasks is easier to accomplish than one giant task.
5. **Set periodic checkpoints.** Stop periodically to ensure you are still on the planned path.
6. **Have a better working environment.** This is ideal advice for avoiding procrastination: Reduce as many distractions and temptations as possible.

One method for setting periodic checkpoints is the [Pomodoro Technique](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/pomodoro-technique), which breaks work into 25-minute chunks punctuated by five-minute breaks.

# Tech Jargon Defined: What is Yak Shaving?

#programming #discuss #productivity #codenewbie

This is part of a Tech Jargon Defined series focused on de-mystifying common tech jargon terms.

'yak shaving', a unique piece of tech jargon, had its origin in an MIT lab, and means executing sub-tasks that seem unrelated to the task at hand but are ultimately necessary to accomplish it. Basically, it's when writing software tickets takes on a 'If You Give a Mouse A Cookie' vibe, but less recursive, and based on needs, not desires. [...] For example, say you had to write a new component for a React project, but the css styles were broken because a dependency was out of date, and to update the dependency you had to update your node version first, and to do that you had to install nvm -- congrats, you're yak shaving. Best comment out the CSS for now and bang out the state logic first. ;)

From: "Jeremy H. Brown"   
 To: all-ai@ai.mit.edu  
 Subject: GSB: 5:30pm, 7ai playroom  
 Date: Fri, 11 Feb 2000 16:00:56 -0500 (EST)  

```

"Yak shaving." Our very own Carlin Vieri invented the term, and yet it has not caught on within the lab. This is a shame, because it describes all too well what I find myself doing all too often.

You see, yak shaving is what you are doing when you're doing some stupid, fiddly little task that bears no obvious relationship to what you're supposed to be working on, but yet a chain of twelve causal relations links what you're doing to the original meta-task.

Here's an example: [...] And that, my friends, is yak shaving. (Not that this particular example happened to me recently or anything.)

Another example of yak shaving might be "I need to ask  a question about our group project. 's hard to track down. But I know  will be at GSB tonight, so I'll go there too." You see, in this case GSB isn't socializing or slacking off, it's part of your work -- hanging out there, you'll be connected to your project via the process of yak shaving! [...] Now, having been introduced to the term and the concept of yak shaving, and also having had it pointed out to you that attending GSB is actually an important part of your research, you are morally bound to come to GSB tonight and discuss the finer points of yak shaving, and in particular the subtle distinctions between some forms of "yak shaving" and "flimsy rationalizations".

 G I R L S C O U T B E N E F I T   5:30pm 7AI Playroom
```

# Yak shaving

[![Bronwyn Boltwood](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/0*80KeJ1kiDYa5Zlcg.png)](https://medium.com/@wyn?source=post_page---byline--3b4bed515a65-----------------------------------------)

[Bronwyn Boltwood](https://medium.com/@wyn?source=post_page---byline--3b4bed515a65-----------------------------------------)

Follow

3 min read

·

Sep 9, 2014

[Listen](https://medium.com/m/signin?actionUrl=https%3A%2F%2Fmedium.com%2Fplans%3Fdimension%3Dpost_audio_button%26postId%3D3b4bed515a65&operation=register&redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmedium.com%2F%40wyn%2Fdefinition-yak-shaving-3b4bed515a65&source=---header_actions--3b4bed515a65---------------------post_audio_button--------------------)

Share

Tangential busywork and necessary-but-nonobvious steps are so hard to tell apart, aren’t they?

I tend to end up telling people about yak shaving sooner or later. “Yak shaving” is hacker slang, defined in the [Jargon File](http://www.catb.org/~esr/jargon/html/Y/yak-shaving.html) as _“any seemingly pointless activity which is actually necessary to solve a problem which solves a problem which, several levels of recursion later, solves the real problem you’re working on.”_ Everyone shaves yaks: we all deal with problems that take _n_ times longer than expected because they had layers like an onion or matryoshka doll.

Some yak shaving is driven by the tendency to optimize and perfect. People are forever saying things like “perfect is the enemy of done,” which is true, but the opposing truth is that good structure, templating, and automation is faster _overall_ on work that you repeat or reuse, often dramatically so. Software developers also know how often they turn out to repeat/reuse work that they expected to be a one-off, or a prototype only. The first three projects or so where I needed to remove backgrounds from images, I fudged my way through fresh each time. On round three where I had worked out a good method, _I wrote it down_ because surely I would need it again. These days, I have to be awfully confident that the task is a one-off before I _skip_ basic optimization steps.

## Get Bronwyn Boltwood’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe

Subscribe

Remember me for faster sign in

Seth Godin gave a delightful example [that actually ends with shaving a yak](http://sethgodin.typepad.com/seths_blog/2005/03/dont_shave_that.html):

> _Yak Shaving is the last step of a series of steps that occurs when you find something you need to do. “I want to wax the car today.”_
>
> _“Oops, the hose is still broken from the winter. I’ll need to buy a new one at Home Depot.”_
>
> _“But Home Depot is on the other side of the Tappan Zee bridge and getting there without my EZPass is miserable because of the tolls.”_
>
> _“But, wait! I could borrow my neighbor’s EZPass…”_
>
> _“Bob won’t lend me his EZPass until I return the mooshi pillow my son borrowed, though.”_
>
> _“And we haven’t returned it because some of the stuffing fell out and we need to get some yak hair to restuff it.”_
>
> _And the next thing you know, you’re at the zoo, shaving a yak, all so you can wax your car._
>
> _This yak shaving phenomenon tends to hit some people more than others, but what makes it particularly perverse is when groups of people get involved. It’s bad enough when one person gets all up in arms yak shaving, but when you try to get a group of people together, you’re just as likely to end up giving the yak a manicure._
>
> _Which is why solo entrepreneurs and small organizations are so much more likely to get stuff done. They have fewer yaks to shave._
>
> _So, what to do?_
>
> _Don’t go to Home Depot for the hose._
>
> _The minute you start walking down a path toward a yak shaving party, it’s worth making a compromise. Doing it well now is much better than doing it perfectly later._

And there at the end is the difficulty. You might be able to cut out the yak shaving on a single task — the fellow waxing the car should have gone to a different hardware store or borrowed a hose — but in a complex project? Count on some yaks. Concentrate on figuring out which path contains the fewest, most co-operative yaks, and how to shave them as efficiently as possible. The first is strategic consulting; the second is technical expertise. Both together? That’s project management, isn’t it?
